bibliography.title: Premise Selection for a Lean Hammer

abstract_sentences.text: Neural methods are transforming automated reasoning for proof assistants, yet integrating these advances into practical verification workflows remains challenging.

evidence.anchor: integrating these advances into practical verification workflows remains challenging

abstract_sentences.text: A hammer is a tool that integrates premise selection, translation to external automatic theorem provers, and proof reconstruction into one overarching tool to automate tedious reasoning steps.

evidence.anchor: integrates premise selection, translation, and proof reconstruction

abstract_sentences.text: We present LeanPremise, a novel neural premise selection system, and we combine it with existing translation and proof reconstruction components to create LeanHammer, the first end-to-end domain general hammer for the Lean proof assistant.

evidence.anchor: the first end-to-end domain general hammer for the Lean proof assistant

abstract_sentences.text: Unlike existing Lean premise selectors, LeanPremise is specifically trained for use with a hammer in dependent type theory.

evidence.anchor: specifically trained for use with a hammer in dependent type theory

abstract_sentences.text: It also dynamically adapts to user-specific contexts, enabling it to effectively recommend premises from libraries outside LeanPremise’s training data as well as lemmas defined by the user locally.

evidence.anchor: recommend premises from libraries outside LeanPremise’s training data

abstract_sentences.text: With comprehensive evaluations, we show that LeanPremise enables LeanHammer to solve 21% more goals than existing premise selectors and generalizes well to diverse domains.

evidence.anchor: solve 21% more goals than existing premise selectors

abstract_sentences.text: Our work helps bridge the gap between neural retrieval and symbolic reasoning, making formal verification more accessible to researchers and practitioners.

final_judgment.single_storyline: The single storyline changes retrieval labels from next-tactic locality to premises sufficient for whole-proof hammer completion, then sends one selector output through Aesop and Lean-auto/Zipperposition/Duper and evaluates theorem-level proof rate (p.5 §3.2.2 “close the goal (all tactics)”; pp.3–4 §3.1; p.8 §4.2).
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The body keeps the pipeline figure, normalized extraction and API mechanism, the two core equations, runtime, Tables 2–4, six miniCTX splits, failure categories, and the reproducibility statement, preserving the decisions about recall-to-proof conversion, cost, generalization, and scope (pp.4–10 Figure 1, Tables 2–4, §§3–5).
final_judgment.appendix_moves: No appendix is present. Signature/pipeline examples, k tuning, baseline details, Figure 2a, Table 5, and D.4/D.5 failure analyses are deferred to Zhu et al. (2025), which leaves the main tables readable but weakens independent audit of tuning, examples, and failure decomposition (pp.4–5 §§3.1–3.2; pp.7–9 §§4.1–4.3).
final_judgment.best_pattern: The strongest pattern is the aligned ladder of Figure 1 information flow, Table 2 retrieval plus five proof settings, None/Ground-truth controls, and Table 4 component deletions; it links a selector change to an executable proof outcome (p.4 Figure 1; p.8 Table 2; pp.9–10 Table 4).
final_judgment.largest_gap: Dynamic local-premise capability is specified by the API and Table 1 but lacks a dedicated local-lemma insertion or context-shift experiment; “first”, “robust”, and “accessible” also lack exhaustive novelty, user, or seed/uncertainty evidence, while failure categories are not quantified by denominator (p.6 §3.3.2; p.7 §4.1; p.9 §4.2).
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For neural retrieval inside a symbolic proof system, train labels against the final verifiable objective (all premises used by the whole proof) and evaluate the same retriever inside proof reconstruction; retrieval recall or next-tactic utility alone cannot establish hammer capability (p.5 §3.2.2; p.8 §4.2).
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This rule applies to hammer/retrieval systems with an explicit premise set, proof reconstruction, and theorem-level success criterion; it does not establish whole-proof generation, induction/arithmetic ability, user adoption, or transfer to other proof assistants (p.3 §2.2; p.9 §4.2; p.7 §4.1).
